title: Wi-Fi encryption
starter: Shift every letter of MEET AT NOON forward by 5 places. Swap with a partner and decode theirs. What would make this code harder to crack?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Why encrypt?
facts: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it.
Wi-Fi signals travel through the air, so anyone in range could intercept them.
Encrypted data is useless to anyone without the key.
stations.challenge: What is the purpose of encryption?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Encryption scrambles data so only someone with the key can read it.
Also credit: Wi-Fi signals travel through the air, so anyone in range could intercept them.

questions.q: What is the purpose of encryption?
questions.a: To scramble data so only someone with the key can understand it

questions.q: Why is encryption especially important for wireless networks?
questions.a: Radio signals can be picked up by anyone within range

stations.name: ROT13 and the Romans
facts: A substitution cipher replaces each letter with another one, using a rule or key.
ROT13 moves each letter 13 places: A becomes N. Doing it twice gives the original back.
Julius Caesar used a shift cipher to send secret messages.
stations.challenge: Decode this ROT13 message: URYYB JBEYQ
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A substitution cipher replaces each letter with another one, using a rule or key.
Also credit: ROT13 moves each letter 13 places: A becomes N. Doing it twice gives the original back.

questions.a: Anyone who knows the rule can reverse it, because there's no secret key

stations.name: Keys
facts: The key is the secret used to encrypt and decrypt a message.
Without the key, the message is very hard to work out.
If a key is sent with the message it could be intercepted, so master keys are known but never sent.
stations.challenge: Why is it risky to send the key along with the message?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The key is the secret used to encrypt and decrypt a message.
Also credit: Without the key, the message is very hard to work out.

questions.a: The secret value used to encrypt and decrypt data

questions.q: Why are master keys never sent over the network?
questions.a: They could be intercepted, and then all the data could be decrypted

stations.name: Public and private keys
facts: A public key can be shared with anyone; it's used to encrypt messages sent to you.
Only your matching private key can decrypt them.
So the private key is never shared with anyone.
stations.challenge: Why must a private key never be shared?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A public key can be shared with anyone; it's used to encrypt messages sent to you.
Also credit: Only your matching private key can decrypt them.

questions.q: Which key can be shared with anyone?
What happens if someone gets hold of your private key?
questions.a: They can decrypt messages meant only for you

stations.name: The WPA2 handshake
facts: Before any data is sent, the device and the access point check each other.
Both work out the same master key from the Wi-Fi password.
They swap random numbers to calculate a temporary key, without ever sending the key itself.
stations.challenge: Why is the master key never sent over the air?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Before any data is sent, the device and the access point check each other.
Also credit: Both work out the same master key from the Wi-Fi password.

questions.q: Put the steps of the Wi-Fi handshake in order.
questions.a: Both devices work out the same master key from the Wi-Fi password → The access point sends a random number to the device → The device uses the random numbers and addresses to calculate a session key → The device replies with its own random number and a check value → The access point calculates the same session key → The access point sends the shared group key, protected by a check value → The device acknowledges, and encrypted data can begin

questions.q: What does WPA2 do before any data is sent?
questions.a: Checks that both devices know the same key, so they can trust each other

stations.name: Staying safe on Wi-Fi
facts: Use networks protected with WPA2 or WPA3.
Open networks with no password send data without Wi-Fi encryption.
A strong Wi-Fi password matters, because the master key is made from it.
stations.challenge: Why is it risky to use online banking on an open café network?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Use networks protected with WPA2 or WPA3.
Also credit: Open networks with no password send data without Wi-Fi encryption.

questions.q: Which network is the safest to use?
questions.a: One protected with WPA2 or WPA3 and a strong password

questions.q: Why does the strength of the Wi-Fi password matter?
questions.a: The master key is made from it, so a weak password makes the key easier to guess

final.name: Final challenge: code breakers

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.a: Plaintext → The original, readable message; Ciphertext → The scrambled message; Key → The secret used to encrypt and decrypt; Public key → Shared with anyone and used to encrypt; Private key → Kept secret and used to decrypt; Encryption → Scrambling data so it can't be read without the key

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
